analysis.one_liner: Blocks FDA from enforcing its rule regulating laboratory-developed tests as medical devices.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, February 21, 2025, and the committee has taken no further action; the FDA rule it targets has not been blocked.
analysis.plain_summary: In May 2024, the FDA finalized a rule saying that laboratory-developed tests — medical tests that laboratories design and run in-house rather than buy from a test manufacturer — are medical devices and must follow FDA rules, with limited exceptions. This bill would forbid any federal money from being used to put that rule into effect or enforce it, and would apply the same ban to any future FDA rule that is substantially similar. In effect, it stops the FDA from overseeing the accuracy of these in-house lab tests.
analysis.who_benefits: Clinical laboratories that develop their own tests — hospital labs, academic medical center labs, and large commercial labs — would be spared the cost and time of FDA registration, premarket review, and quality requirements for the tests they build in-house. This matters because lab-developed tests are a large and growing part of the testing market, including cancer and genetic testing.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any use of federal funds to implement, administer, or enforce the FDA's final rule titled "Medical Devices; Laboratory Developed Tests" published May 6, 2024, or any substantially similar rule.

The targeted rule had specified that laboratory-developed tests are medical devices subject to FDA regulation, with limited exceptions — meaning labs would have to meet device requirements for the tests they design and run in-house.
Blocking enforcement spares laboratories the cost of FDA submissions and quality-system compliance for their in-house tests, a burden that manufacturers of off-the-shelf test kits already carry.

analysis.who_pays: Patients who rely on laboratory-developed test results would bear the added risk: their tests would not go through FDA review of accuracy before use, unlike the manufactured test kits the FDA already regulates. The FDA would also lose its role as a backstop for test quality.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients relying on lab test results

drawbacks.text: Before the 2024 rule, the FDA had exercised discretion over whether to apply medical device regulation to laboratory-developed tests, meaning many such tests reached patients without FDA review.
The funding ban would also cover any "substantially similar" future FDA rule, so the agency could not write a new version of the oversight rule either.

Patients use laboratory-developed tests for major medical decisions such as cancer screening and genetic risk; blocking FDA oversight leaves the accuracy of those tests to the labs' own internal quality controls, with no outside check equivalent to the review manufactured test kits receive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill saves laboratories real compliance costs, and a fair objection is that FDA regulation could raise the price of specialized tests or make some rare-disease tests harder to offer. But the bill removes the FDA's accuracy review of in-house lab tests without putting any alternative quality standard in its place, and it would even bar the FDA from writing a rewritten rule later. The savings go to the labs; the accuracy risk sits with patients.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote since.

narrative.text: Representative Brad Finstad introduced the bill in the House on February 21, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
The committee has taken no further action on the bill, and no vote has been held in either chamber.
Because no law has been enacted, the FDA's May 2024 laboratory-developed tests rule has not been blocked by Congress.
The bill had seven cosponsors, all House Republicans, as of the congressional record of the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one's position has changed: the bill has not advanced, so the FDA rule it targets has not been blocked, and laboratories have gained nothing from it through Congress. Patients remain under the status quo, in which FDA oversight of these tests depends on the contested rule's fate in court rather than in Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo — the FDA rule stands

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and has taken no further recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors are House Republicans, no Democrat has signed on, and no vote has been held to show broader support.

industries.industry: Clinical laboratories (hospital, academic, and commercial labs that develop their own tests)
industries.note: The bill would spare these labs the FDA device requirements — registration, premarket review, and quality rules — that the 2024 rule applied to their in-house tests. Their gain comes from avoiding an accuracy-oversight process that protects the patients taking the tests.

industries.industry: Manufacturers of off-the-shelf diagnostic test kits
industries.note: Kit manufacturers already meet FDA medical device requirements, and the 2024 rule would have applied similar requirements to their lab-based competitors. Blocking the rule preserves the labs' lighter regulatory footing, which keeps kit makers at a relative disadvantage rather than removing their own obligations.

industries.industry: FDA-regulated diagnostics oversight as a public function
industries.note: A funding ban would strip the FDA of any means to enforce the laboratory-developed tests rule or a similar future rule, ending the agency's planned backstop on test accuracy. The public relies on that review for tests used in cancer and genetic medicine.

analysis.trajectory: With only eight Republican backers, no Democratic cosponsors, and no committee action since the February 2025 referral, the bill is unlikely to receive a standalone vote this Congress. Bills of this type typically advance only if attached to a broader spending or FDA-related package. Separately, industry groups have challenged the FDA rule in court, so the rule's fate may be decided by judges rather than by this bill.
